doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Composition as selective improvisation
summary: Brubeck discusses Stravinsky's idea that composing is selective improvisation, how he writes melody first and harmonizes, and Milhaud's ability to write without a piano.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you compose, was it Stravinsky who said something about composing is selective improvisation?
Does that have anything to do with the way you write?

Probably. It’s an interesting book, Stravinsky, Poetics of Music. And that’s I think one of the most important sentences that a musician, a young musician, should really look at and try and digest because selective improvisation — composition is selective improvisation. And that connects the composer and the jazz musician in a wonderful way in that it’s the same kind of mindset that plays jazz as composes and writes music. But you haven’t got time to be selective. You have to move to the next note in a split second. And in composition you can stop and go have lunch or put it away for a few years. So selective, but it’s the same kind of thinking, only on a quicker level. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
Yeah. You can go back and edit things that you might have done on the spot and you liked part of it perhaps.
If I was to look at an orchestral score and look down the page vertically, do you think in chordal structure when you write these days?
Well usually I first think of a melodic line. And then I harmonize it. And I have to write on the road in airplanes and trains and buses and cars. And then I check it later.
At the piano? To see if—

Yes. To see if I’m close to right. And I know that my teacher Darius Milhaud never had to check anything and never had to be near a piano, and like a Mozart his mind worked, just some kind of perfection that God gave a few people. Stravinsky always wrote at the piano.
That’s interesting. The ideas that you’ve had in jazz, the polytonality and polyrhythmic, do you try to get those into your orchestral pieces also?
Always, yeah. They’re always floating around there.
